claims.text: Enhanced atomic-scale homogeneity results in higher configurational entropy in multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Greater atomic-scale homogeneity improves high-temperature structural and chemical stability.
Suppressed elemental diffusion and segregation cause the proposed improvement in high-temperature stability.
High-energy physical vapor deposition promotes uniform elemental mixing in these nanoparticles.
Chemical reduction tends to produce a less uniform elemental distribution than physical vapor deposition.
Changing the synthesis route from physical vapor deposition to chemical reduction isolates the effects of mixing homogeneity and configurational entropy on stability.
Atomic-scale chemical homogeneity determines local elemental clustering and the propensity for phase segregation during thermal stress.
High configurational entropy from uniform mixing increases kinetic barriers to elemental diffusion.
Suppressing atomic migration minimizes segregation and phase separation.
Physical-vapor-deposited nanoparticles will undergo minimal changes in phase composition and elemental distribution after exposure at 773–1173 K.
Chemically reduced nanoparticles with lower homogeneity will show more segregation, phase separation, or degradation than the physical-vapor-deposited nanoparticles.
Standard synthesis routes typically produce moderate mixing.
A moderate degree of mixing produces an intermediate degree of structural deterioration under the stated service conditions.
The proposed relationship is limited to multi-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under catalytic conditions at 773–1173 K.
Surface oxidation or other dominant factors may override the proposed homogeneity-based stabilization mechanism.
Comparable degradation in the two nanoparticle sets would falsify the proposed protective effect of enhanced homogeneity and configurational entropy.
